questions.question: What does the Heine-Borel Theorem say for a subset $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: $\boldsymbol{E}$ is compact if and only if it is open and connected.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is compact if and only if it is finite.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is compact if and only if it is a vector space.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.

questions.question: In the interpretation, what role does boundedness play?
options: It ensures that the set contains no boundary points.
It makes every function on the set continuous.
It forces the set to be a line.
It keeps the set from running off to infinity.

questions.question: Which set is compact in $\mathbb{R}^n$ by the examples?
Why is the closed metric ball $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)$ compact in Euclidean space?
Which statement is a key consequence involving compact sets?
options: The continuous image of a compact set is compact.
The continuous image of any set is compact.
Every bounded set is compact in every metric space.

questions.question: Which operation on compact sets is guaranteed to preserve compactness?
Let $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be closed but unbounded. What can be concluded from Heine-Borel?
Let $\boldsymbol{K}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be compact and let $\boldsymbol{A}\subseteq\boldsymbol{K}$ be closed. what is true about $\boldsymbol{A}$?
Which misuse of Heine-Borel is ruled out by the Euclidean-space hypothesis?
options: Using closedness and boundedness for subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Assuming closed and bounded implies compact in every metric space.
Checking compactness of a closed interval in $\mathbb{R}$.
Treating a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as compact.

questions.question: Which statement correctly combines Heine-Borel with the extreme value theorem mentioned?
options: Every function on a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ attains extrema.
Every continuous function on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ attains extrema, in all instances without exception.
A continuous real-valued function on a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ attains extrema.
A closed subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ must contain only finitely many points.

In the interpretation of Heine-Borel, what does boundedness prevent?
options: The set from containing its boundary.
The set from being a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

questions.question: Which subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is compact by Heine-Borel?

options: It is not a subset of Euclidean space.

questions.question: Which property fails for $[0,+\infty)\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ to be compact by Heine-Borel?
Which operation on compact sets is guaranteed for finite families?
options: Finite unions of compact sets are never compact.
Finite unions of compact sets must be empty.
Finite unions of compact sets are compact.
Finite unions of compact sets must be open.
